name: Emergency Substitute Plans
title: Emergency Substitute Plans
answer: Emergency substitute plans are ready-made lesson plans a teacher keeps on hand for unexpected absences, drafted with AI help so a stranger can follow them. They matter because they protect both learning and students when the teacher cannot be there, and they need periodic review because routines and students change.

sections.body: This idea addresses the scramble that follows an unexpected teacher absence, when a substitute arrives with little to work from. AI can help draft plans that a stranger can follow, with clear instructions, materials, and routines. A teacher might keep several ready at the start of the year. The plans should connect to what students are learning rather than just fill time. The problem it solves is the gap between a sudden absence and a day that still holds together for students.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, a teacher prepares several substitute plans at the start of the year and stores them for use when an absence cannot be planned. Each plan gives the substitute clear instructions, materials, and routines, and it ties to what students are currently learning instead of serving as busywork. The plan includes what the substitute needs to know without sharing private details, states how students with accommodations receive their supports without naming disabilities, and makes safety procedures and whom to contact clear. Teachers review their plans every few months, since routines and students change and a plan written in August may not fit in February. The text does not give grade band variations.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no evidence label, study, or figure for this idea. It rests on practice rather than research, and the book presents it as a practical routine for teachers rather than a finding backed by data.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The plan must include information the substitute needs without sharing private details. Students with accommodations still need their supports provided, but the plan can say what to do without naming disabilities. Safety procedures and whom to contact should be clear. Teachers should review their plans every few months, because routines change, students change, and a plan written in August may not fit in February. The decisions about what goes into the plan and when to update it stay with the teacher.
